assumptions: The initial offer is limited to genuinely difficult or ambiguous product-classification cases, not commodity code lookup that public sources and existing automation already address.

Qualified customs specialists can be contracted to own professional opinions, escalations, and any regulated representation under applicable Polish and EU conditions, although their cost, availability, insurance, and liability allocation remain unknown.

The intended first channel is a smaller freight forwarder or customs agency without a capable internal classification stack; no exclusivity, embedded workflow access, or minimum case volume is assumed.
Private product facts and case outcomes are reused only with explicit contractual permission and effective de-identification; no proprietary data right is assumed before those contracts exist.
The proposed pricing, case volume, gross margin, acquisition payback, workspace retention, and founder-net-worth path are planning hypotheses rather than validated performance.
The founder can keep the business within the stated part-time limit only if contracted specialists handle client-specific customs judgment and operational escalations as proposed.
evidence_needed_for_higher_score: Paid pilots with several capability-poor forwarders or importers showing monthly difficult-case volume, conversion at the proposed case price, actual specialist and liability costs, contribution margin and cash collection, workspace renewal, decision-quality or time savings versus incumbents, and signed permission to reuse de-identified outcomes; a scoped legal and insurance opinion on the operating model is also needed.

factors.name: Core insight
factors.rationale: The opportunity correctly distinguishes high-value product-fact development, expert reasoning, audit trails, and exception support from generic tariff-code prediction. Classification can affect duties, licences, restrictions, and validity of a BTI, so there is a consequential decision to improve. The proposed private outcome cooperative is a plausible refinement, but its incremental value over public rulings and incumbent knowledge bases is still unknown.

factors.name: Customer pain and willingness to pay
factors.rationale: A wrong classification can create duty, compliance, delay, and annulment exposure, making difficult cases materially painful. Existing managed classification and forwarder consulting offers support a realistic basis for paid help. However, the Polish application and decision are free, and there is no direct evidence for the proposed 2,000-12,000 PLN case fee, workspace subscription, or target-forwarder case frequency.

factors.name: Business model and economics
factors.rationale: Case fees plus recurring workflow access could combine early services revenue with software leverage, and the stated initial capital is within the founder's available capital. Yet the claimed 55%-80% gross margin, 8-16 month payback, retention, expert-review cost, insurance burden, CAC, and 3 million PLN ARR path are all unvalidated. Free official filing, expert labor, client follow-up, appeal support, and a slow ruling cycle could leave the model service-heavy with weak cash conversion and limited operating leverage.

factors.name: Market and beachhead
factors.rationale: Novel or ambiguous EU imports create a recurring and economically meaningful problem domain, and smaller forwarders lacking internal capability are a potentially reachable starting segment. The proposed beachhead is not yet specified tightly enough by product category, loss profile, geography, or minimum case density, and no evidence quantifies the number of qualifying buyers or cases needed to support a focused business.

factors.name: Competitive position and domination potential
factors.rationale: Avalara, eClear, and TariffPilot already offer overlapping automation, reasoning, APIs, bulk workflow, and in some cases human expertise, while Maersk demonstrates that a forwarder can internalize the consulting offer. The candidate has no bound channel, exclusive expertise, vertical specialization, or proven outcome advantage that would presently support a particularly strong position in its beachhead.

factors.name: Expansion potential
factors.rationale: A trusted classification workflow and specialist network could extend across more EU geographies, product families, appeals, audits, landed-cost analysis, and adjacent customs-compliance decisions. Those adjacencies are logically available, but they remain prospective and may add country-specific legal, expert, and data requirements before the initial wedge has been proven.

factors.name: Defensibility and durability
factors.rationale: Consented private mappings from facts and questions to rulings, appeals, and realized costs could improve retrieval and expert productivity over time. Defensibility is weak at present because rulings and core official research are public, outcome feedback can take at least 120 days after acceptance, private-data reuse rights are uncertain, and larger software vendors and forwarders may accumulate more workflow data and relationships.

factors.name: Strength of advantage
factors.rationale: For difficult products, a complete expert-reviewed evidence pack with an audit trail and exception support could be more trustworthy and convenient than self-service research. The packet provides no evidence that this offer is materially faster, cheaper, more accurate, safer, or easier to buy than incumbent managed services and forwarder consulting, so a behavior-changing advantage is not yet established.

factors.name: Timing and momentum
factors.rationale: AI can reduce evidence retrieval and workflow costs while tariff sources change frequently and classification complexity persists. The same technology is already being deployed by established competitors and commoditizes simple cases; the evidence identifies no new regulatory, channel, or customer-behavior catalyst that uniquely favors this entrant now.

factors.name: Distribution
factors.rationale: Embedding at a forwarder's new-SKU intake is well aligned with the problem trigger and could aggregate repeat cases without requiring a broad consumer brand. But willingness to embed, white-label, share data, or grant exclusivity is unknown, and forwarders can sell classification themselves. The route is plausible for smaller capability-poor partners but is not yet repeatable, affordable, or controlled.

factors.name: Execution and risks
factors.rationale: The founder's data, AI, and workflow skills fit the tooling layer, and the estimated capital is affordable. Execution nonetheless depends on qualified specialists, accurate and confidential product facts, representation rules, empowerment, insurance and liability allocation, data-use consent, and partner operations. Part-time feasibility exists only if those specialists own judgment and escalations, which is not yet evidenced.

highest_value_structural_change: Own the customer and data right in one demonstrably high-loss, repeat-SKU importer niche: sell an annual expert-backed classification evidence and monitoring contract directly to importers, contract for de-identified outcome reuse, and treat forwarders as integration or referral endpoints rather than the indispensable channel. This would reduce channel conflict, concentrate expertise and cases, and make the proposed data advantage more controllable.
main_structural_strength: The offer attaches to a consequential new-SKU or dispute trigger and focuses on expert-reviewed fact development and defensible case evidence, a layer for which free official filing and generic code automation do not eliminate customer value.
primary_score_limiter: The proposed control point is not owned: forwarders are expected to provide distribution and case data while some can deliver the service themselves, and no channel agreement, exclusive niche, or contractual outcome-data right currently prevents substitution.
strongest_disconfirming_evidence: Mature vendors already combine tariff automation, APIs, bulk workflow, reasoned outputs, and human expertise, while Maersk already sells HS-classification consulting through the intended channel; this directly challenges both differentiation and the forwarder-embedded acquisition thesis.
